"Grippy McGee" gripper FEA in Ansys Mechanical · Oct 2026

My first FEA project · independent
A static structural analysis of the arm's gripper at servo stall in Ansys Workbench/Mechanical 2026 R1. A DS3240 servo drives a 15T pinion and two counter-rotating 60T gears, which turn cranks in a parallelogram four-bar so the TPU-padded jaws stay parallel as they close. The goal: hold the 5 kg CIRC payload without breaking.

The first analysis showed the PLA-CF cranks would fail (SF 0.53). That drove a redesign, and the corrected CAD now reaches SF 3.3 and meets the 5 kg requirement.

Before and after: the FEA drove the redesign

DS3240 at stallOld CADCorrected CAD
Crank stress (realistic)72.3 MPa · SF 0.53, fails11.6 MPa · SF 3.3
Squeeze force per claw~103 N~117 N
Fore-aft drag per claw~100 N~23 N
Payload held (μ 0.5, ×2 dynamic)~5.2 kg~6 kg
Max deformation1.35 mm0.17 mm

Bulkier cranks and rockers, new jaw geometry and a closed claw-plate gap cut crank stress about 6× and turned most of the jaw force into useful squeeze.

Corrected CAD results

Grip force
±117 N squeeze per claw
Payload held
~6 kg with ×2 dynamic factor: meets CIRC
Crank SF
3.3 realistic · 1.6 at the spike
Weakest part
15T pinion, Lewis SF ≈ 1.13
  • Built the model: imported the Onshape assemblies, entered 5 datasheet materials (PLA-CF, TPU 95A, Al 6061-T6, 303 and 1045 steel), and replaced bonded contacts with revolute joints (fixed joints between crank halves) so the linkage could move.
  • Worked within the Student license: meshed down from ~836K to ~122–126K nodes, removed the gears and applied the equivalent crank torque (T = 4414 × 60/15 ÷ 2 = 8830 N·mm), and checked the gear teeth by hand with the Lewis bending equation.
  • Validated: old-CAD claw forces matched the 141.7 N hand calculation within ~1%. The corrected CAD reads ~15% lower (121 N vs 142 N), as expected from the extra constraint at each jaw. Global equilibrium and left/right symmetry both check out.
  • Recommendations: print Gear Link 3 flat and add a brass or steel bushing at the pin hole, and upgrade the 15T pinion (hardened steel or module 1.5), the weakest gear at SF ≈ 1.13.

Case 2: holding the 5 kg CIRC payload

Can the gripper hold the heaviest CIRC object while the arm moves it? I modeled the worst pose, with the gripper horizontal and the arm outstretched, so the payload bends the jaws sideways. The load was 5 kg × 9.81 × 2 (dynamic factor) = 98 N, or 49 N down per claw, with the servo still at stall. The object was modeled as a support that holds each claw only in the squeeze direction, so the payload pulls down on it like friction from a real object.

Case 2 resultValueVerdict
Squeeze per claw110–114 NBoth jaws gripping
Slip check (μ ≈ 0.5)56 N available vs 49 N needed · margin 1.14Holds 5 kg, thin margin
Crank stress (realistic)10.3 MPa · SF 3.7 in-layer, 2.5 acrossStrong enough
Crank peak in plot35.3 MPa at one node; 4.3–4.8 MPa 2–3 mm awayModeling artifact
Jaw-tip sag5.2 mm (×2 dynamic) · ~2.6 mm staticMain weakness
Load into the arm107 N vertical + 18.4 N·m bendingHanded to the arm team
  • Validated: the mount reaction of 106.9 N matches the hand calculation (98 N payload + ~9 N gripper = 107 N), the side forces sum to zero, and the 18.4 N·m moment matches 98 N × ~0.18 m.
  • Strong enough, not stiff enough: each jaw plate is only 5 mm thick and ~148 mm long, and the soft TPU pad doesn't tie the top and bottom plates together, so they bend almost independently.
  • Thin friction margin: a slippery or wet object (μ below ~0.44) could slip.
  • Next CAD revision: tie the jaw plates together near the tips with rigid standoffs so each jaw acts as a stiff box section, and add texture or a higher-friction pad.

Case 3: thermal at CIRC, hot day and typical day

Do the 3D-printed parts get too hot at CIRC (Drumheller, Alberta, in August)? PLA-CF's heat deflection temperature is 54 °C, and dark carbon-fiber prints absorb most of the sunlight. I linked a steady-state thermal analysis to the Case 1 model and applied 900 W/m² of sun on the top surfaces, convection plus linearized radiation (h ≈ 22 W/m²·K) on every surface, and a stalled servo held 20 °C above ambient. I ran two climates: a 40 °C heat wave and a 24 °C typical August day.

PLA-CF locationHot day (40 °C)Typical day (24 °C)
Max · base plate top65.6 °C49.6 °C
Crank and rocker tops60.4–65.4 °C46.5–49.2 °C
Servo tower top65.0 °C~48.5 °C
Top jaw plate near tip62.1 °C~46 °C
Shaded back and bottom plates40–52 °C24–36 °C
vs 54 °C HDT6–12 °C over on sunlit load partsUnder, only ~4 °C margin
  • Validated: a hand calculation for a sunlit plate cooled on both faces gives ΔT = 900 / (2 × 22) ≈ 20 °C, or ~60 °C on a 40 °C day, versus 60–65 °C in the FEA. Dropping every temperature input by 16 °C dropped every result by exactly 16.0 °C, confirming the linear model.
  • Modeling choice: a full nonlinear radiation boundary stalled in pre-processing, so I linearized radiation as h_rad = 4εσT³ ≈ 7 W/m²·K, which is accurate over the 20–80 °C range.
  • Finding: on a hot, sunny day the sunlit load-carrying parts (cranks, rockers, top plate and top jaw plates) exceed PLA-CF's HDT and could creep while gripping at stall. On a typical day PLA-CF works, but with little margin.
  • Recommendations: reprint those parts in a higher-temperature filament (PETG-CF, ASA-CF or nylon-CF, checking each HDT against ~65 °C), use a light color or reflective cover on top surfaces, and keep the gripper shaded between tasks.
  • Limitations: steady state, constant material properties and no thermal-stress coupling. A natural next step is importing these temperatures into Case 1.

Stiffen and tie the jaw plates together, add grippier pads, upgrade the 15T pinion, and reprint the sunlit load-carrying parts in a higher-temperature filament.

Debugging the model

  • Fixed a moment applied between the two crank halves instead of crank-to-frame, a floating frame part traced to suppressed contacts, and auto-connection refresh silently re-creating contacts. I mapped every pin axis from the STEP file with a script to check the joints.
  • Caught my own input error: early runs used an MG996R (1.08 N·m) instead of the DS3240 in the CAD (4.41 N·m). The re-run scaled exactly ×4.09, which confirmed the model, and showed the MG996R could only hold ~1.3 kg.

Bio-inspired Underwater Vehicle

Undergraduate Student Researcher · Jan 2026 – Present
BRL-AUVSolidWorks · Tank testing

An autonomous underwater vehicle for structural inspection in the Chesapeake Bay. The design puts hydrodynamic efficiency and a reliable seal first. I own all of the SolidWorks CAD and 3D-print the hull, with a flexible TPU tail for propulsion.

  • Designed and built the vehicle from concept to a working prototype in 2 weeks across 2 iterations, guided by 10+ peer-reviewed studies on dolphin fin kinematics.
  • Engineered a split hull with internal mounts to integrate and package sensors, motors and electronics within a 2 × 2 × 2 ft envelope, cutting assembly time by 5%.
  • Developed the hull and tail propulsion design: prototyped a mold-injected fin, then moved to a flexible TPU tail.
  • Packaged sensors and motor drives into compact pressure housings, with CAD layouts that balance buoyancy and keep electronics dry.
  • Planned and ran sealing, structural and buoyancy tests, performed root cause and corrective action (RCCA) on water leaks, and made corrective design changes until the hull was fully watertight.
